walkthroughs.body_html:
Religion & Ethics: Applied Ethics (Euthanasia, Business Ethics, Sexual Ethics) — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religion & Ethics: Applied Ethics (Euthanasia, Business Ethics, Sexual Ethics) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religion & Ethics: Applied Ethics (Euthanasia, Business Ethics, Sexual Ethics).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between active and passive euthanasia?
options: Active involves a deliberate act to end life, such as a lethal dose; passive involves withdrawing or withholding treatment
Active is legal in the UK while passive is not
Active applies only to animals
There is no recognised difference

mcqs.q: What does the sanctity of life principle claim?
options: Life is intrinsically valuable and God-given, so it should not be deliberately ended
Life's value depends entirely on its usefulness
Only healthy lives have value
Human and animal lives are identical in worth

mcqs.q: What did Milton Friedman argue about business?
options: A business's social responsibility is to increase its profits within the rules of the game
Businesses must prioritise charity over profit
Profit-making is inherently immoral
Companies should be run by religious leaders

mcqs.q: What does the doctrine of double effect permit?
options: An action with a foreseen bad side effect, if the intended effect is good and proportionate - such as pain relief that may shorten life
Any action with two effects
Deliberate killing if the motive is kind
Lying whenever it is convenient

mcqs.q: Is withdrawing futile treatment the same as euthanasia in UK law?
options: No - withdrawing burdensome or futile treatment in a patient's best interests is lawful medical practice, while deliberately administering a lethal dose remains illegal.
Utilitarianism forbids all medical treatment.
Doctors who withdraw treatment are committing euthanasia under UK law.
All forms of euthanasia are legal in the UK.
Utilitarianism forbids all medical treatment.
All forms of euthanasia are legal in the UK.
A utilitarian must always approve a request for euthanasia.

No - the calculation could go either way: relief of suffering counts in favour, but effects on families, trust in doctors and slippery-slope risks count against; the theory fixes a method, not a verdict.

mcqs.q: Is whistle-blowing always an act of disloyalty?
options: Not necessarily - Kantian honesty and stakeholder arguments hold that preventing serious harm can override loyalty, and exposing wrongdoing may serve the firm's genuine long-term interests.
Whistle-blowing refers to refereeing company sports matches.
All forms of euthanasia are legal in the UK.
Employees are morally bound to stay silent about wrongdoing out of loyalty.
